newsitem.title: UK: UK RATE RISE -- Round-up of analyst comment.
newsitem.headline: UK RATE RISE -- Round-up of analyst comment.

text.p: Following is a round-up of economists' comments on Wednesday's quarter-point increase in UK base rates to 6.0 percent:
STUART THOMSON, NIKKO EUROPE

"A politically inspired rate hike. The rate hike is designed to improve the government's credibility. The government is clearly showing that the focus of the election campaign will be the economy and the government's prudent management of the economy. In pre-emptively raising interest rates now, they are getting the Governor on their side."

"We all knew that interest rates would have to rise over the next year but few were actually looking for it today because of the strength of sterling that we've seen in recent months. We've seen more than a five percent rise in sterling's trade-weighted index since August. This has the equivalent monetary impact of a one percent rise in base rates, so monetary conditions have already been tightened and this quarter-percent hike is the icing on the cake. At the IMF meeting last month, Eddie George said he would be content with a quarter-point rise in base rates. He has achieved that objective and I believe that no further interest rate hikes are necessary in the near term."
JONATHAN LOYNES, HSBC MARKETS

"Today's rate increase suggests that Mr Clarke had decided that he could not hold off Mr George's increasingly robust requests for higher rates all the way to the general election, particularly against the background of the disappointing inflation numbers we are likely to see over the next few months. Rather than risk having to raise rates closer to the election, Mr Clarke therefore seems to have decided to get the rise out of the way now and hope that it is largely forgotten by the time of the election. Is this the first of a stream of interest rate hikes? We think not."

"We see this rise as a pre-emptive strike designed to fine-tune the economy and relieve the pressure on Mr Clarke from the Bank of England. The seven percent appreciation of sterling since early August is already quivalent (on the Treasury's rule of thumb) to a monetary tightening of about 1.5 percent and, as long as this strength is sustained, Mr Clarke will be able to claim that a further tightening through higher base rates is unnecessary. Indeed, with manufacturers already struggling to pull out of recession, further rises in rates -- and the further rise in sterling they could precipitate -- could do serious damage to industry."
"Our forecast is now for base rates to hold steady at 6.0 percent until the end of 1997."
ANDREW CATES, UBS

"Clarke's decision to raise base rates today was somewhat surprising given sterling's recent appreciation, still-sluggish conditions in the manufacturing sector and the proximity of the general election. Nevertheless, with consumers on the rampage, GDP growing at an above-trend pace and the underlying inflation rate still above the target ceiling, it was the right decision."

"By acting pre-emptively, this decision will force the Governor into conceding that the chances of hitting the inflation target have improved, so much so that further demands from the Bank for higher base rates are unlikely. As a result we expect base rates to remain unchanged until after the election next year...The major lenders have not raised their mortgage rates following the move...We guess that the Bank of England will next Wednesday lower its inflation forecasts and suggest that base rates need rise no further. Assuming the chancellor delivers a cautious budget, this should allow him to leave base rates where they are until the general election."
RICHARD JEFFREY, CHARTERHOUSE

"I think what the rate increase has served to do is focus the market's attention on the fact that there is potentially more of a problem on inflation than was earlier recognised. If there is a problem -- and the chancellor seems to acknowledge implicitly that it's less likely now that he will get inflation down to 2.5 percent -- then he has got to do more about it. My personal view of the strength of sterling is that its strength is actually telling you a tightening is required. I think rates will probably go up another half a percent in the New Year. If they don't, the gilt market will become increasingly nervous."
ANDREW MILLIGAN, GENERAL ACCIDENT

"The base rate rise to 6.0 percent should be seen as a political decision first and foremost. By doing so the Chancellor protects his flank for the next six months from any accusation that the government is playing fast and loose with its anti-inflation policy...The opinion polls show that the government can benefit from the perception that it is a good manager of the economy; this is an area where the electorate appears to be concerned about Labour...The tightening of monetary policy before the budget does have implications for fiscal policy."

"There have been calls from backbench MPs for significant tax cuts in order to differentiate the party from Labour. The net cut may therefore be more like 4 bln stg rather than 2 bln on November 26...The base rate increase may also suggest that the Treasury's internal RPI forecasts are not too favourable. If the Treasury did think that the RPIX could ease towards 2.5 percent in coming months, why should interest rates be tightened now?"
MICHAEL DICKS, LEHMAN BROTHERS

"It is natural to conclude that the chancellor's reputation for displaying prudence in his management of the economy has been enhanced...Having tightened the monetary stance, he might want to argue that an overall relaxation in the fiscal stance is now warranted. Consequently, the rate hike looks like a prelude to fiscal easing, at least from households' point of view...Such a shift in the policy stance, were it to occur, is by no means the ideal way of dealing with the inflation pressures that the Bank of England has rightly identified."

"The impact of a stronger currency in slowing activity will work through the export-oriented manufacturing ector -- hardly the sector of the economy which needs depressing. Worse still, if the chancellor does decide to go ahead and cut taxes in November's budget, then he will give further impetus to activity by boosting households' take-home pay and, most probably, spending. All in all such a scenario does not look especially optimistic from the point of view of the inflation threat being dealt with satisfactorily."

"Rather, it looks likely that three or four months down the line, we are going to be back to where we were this morning -- with the Bank of England once again calling for higher interest rateas to help prevent inflation remaining above the official target and the markets speculating whether or not the chancellor will once agains display prudence and raise rates again...If the chancellor is actually playing a political game -- and the leopard has not really changed its spots -- then it should be apparent by next spring, if not earlier, that today's rate hike was not the beginning of a sustained move to try to deal with the inflation threat." -- Richard Murphy, 44 171 542 2774
